articles.title: China’s new anti-drone weapon is laser on wheels: Why it matters for modern warfare
articles.summary: International News: China’s People’s Liberation Army (PLA) appears to be developing an amphibious armoured vehicle fitted with a laser weapon and additional sensors to co.
articles.body: China’s People’s Liberation Army (PLA) appears to be developing an amphibious armoured vehicle fitted with a laser weapon and additional sensors to counter drones, potentially giving frontline forces greater protection during a possible Taiwan landing operation. The new variant of the Type 19 8x8 combat vehicle was seen in unverified images posted on Chinese social media on August 29, as Taiwan moves to rapidly expand its own drone capabilities.The development comes as Taipei prepares to spend billions of dollars on uncrewed systems. On September 3, Taiwan’s cabinet proposed a NT$145.7 billion ($4.6 billion) supplementary defence budget that includes more than 600 coastal surveillance and reconnaissance drones and over 40,000 coastal attack drones. The package still needs legislative approval.The combination points to a battlefield in which drones could play a major role on both sides. For PLA forces attempting to land and establish a foothold in Taiwan, a mobile system capable of detecting and disabling drones could help protect troops and armoured vehicles from attacks and surveillance.The Type 19 family is already associated with PLA amphibious formations. Defence intelligence provider Janes reported in 2023 that vehicles from the family had entered service with the 73rd Group Army under the Eastern Theatre Command. The command includes amphibious brigades that would be expected to play a major role in any Taiwan landing operation.If the newly seen vehicle retains the Type 19's amphibious capability, it could potentially accompany troops during an assault and provide short-range protection against uncrewed surveillance aircraft and loitering munitions.Timothy Heath, founder of defence consultancy Perceptum and a former senior China analyst at Rand Corporation and for the US military, said it was difficult to know without more technical data whether the modifications affected the Type 19’s amphibious performance, but he believed operating the laser system while afloat “should be possible”.The vehicle's additional equipment could, however, create technical challenges. The laser, sensors and associated systems would add weight to an amphibious platform where buoyancy is critical. The equipment would also have to withstand exposure to salt water.Heath said the added weight could potentially be offset by reducing the crew size or other equipment, although the system would also need to be protected from salt water.Taiwan is building a large drone forceTaiwan has been expanding its use of uncrewed systems as it prepares for a potential conflict with China. Days before the proposed supplementary budget, Taiwanese lawmakers approved a separate six-year NT$240 billion framework for domestically produced drones after rejecting a competing government plan.The island has also reorganised parts of its military around drone warfare.The army finalised drone battalions across three operational combat zones in April. The marine corps had earlier established a drone battalion as part of a restructuring that also included disbanding tank and self-propelled artillery battalions.During Taiwan's Han Kuang 42 military exercise in August, aerial drone units carried out battlefield surveillance and reconnaissance, intelligence transmission and attack missions, according to the island's defence ministry.For an amphibious force, drones could pose several threats beyond direct attacks. They could track troop movements, identify vehicles and positions and help direct artillery, missiles and other weapons towards exposed forces.That makes a mobile counter-drone system potentially valuable during the most vulnerable phase of a landing operation.Heath said the laser-based counter-drone system could be “very useful in a Taiwan conflict” in which Taiwanese forces might use drone swarms to target amphibious vehicles coming ashore.The cost of firing a laser can also be much lower than repeatedly using conventional missiles or ammunition against relatively inexpensive drones. That could become important in a conflict involving large numbers of uncrewed systems.Heath added that the laser system’s low operating cost could make it particularly useful against such attacks.Lessons from Ukraine and earlier drone warfareThe apparent development also fits a wider shift in military thinking after recent conflicts demonstrated how vulnerable armoured and frontline forces can be to drones.In the Russia-Ukraine war, uncrewed aircraft have been used extensively for reconnaissance, artillery spotting and attacks on tanks, artillery and other military equipment.Heath said the new Type 19 variant was consistent with lessons from the Russia-Ukraine war, where drones had proved effective against tanks, artillery and other frontline targets, increasing the value of mounting counter-drone systems directly on individual platforms.He said the PLA had “almost certainly” drawn similar lessons from earlier fighting between Armenia and Azerbaijan, where drones had shown an ability to bypass traditional air-defence systems.Those lessons appear to be driving a broader PLA effort to protect troops and vehicles from drones. Possible approaches include additional armour, conventional guns and missiles, as well as newer directed-energy systems such as lasers and microwave weapons.The Type 19 could represent another step in that evolution by putting sensors and counter-drone capabilities directly on an armoured vehicle that can move with mechanised formations.Other militaries are pursuing similar concepts.South Korea's Hanwha this week unveiled a Tigon 8x8 armoured vehicle fitted with a 50-kilowatt counter-drone laser. The company has built a prototype and plans serial production by the end of 2027.In the United States, AeroVironment's 20kW-class Locust system has been mounted on Army Joint Light Tactical Vehicles. JLTV-mounted Locust systems were delivered to the US Army in December under a prototyping programme.The PLA system seen in the Type 19 images, however, remains less certain.Janes assessed the vehicle as a Type 19-based counter-drone variant, but it is not clear whether it is operational, undergoing trials or being used only as a technology demonstrator.Why the laser matters, and its limitsA laser could give an amphibious formation a potentially deep magazine against drones because it does not rely on carrying a conventional interceptor for every target. It could also complement existing guns and other air-defence weapons.But directed-energy weapons have limitations.Their effectiveness can be reduced by weather, smoke and dust. They also require substantial electrical power and cooling. These factors could be particularly important during a contested amphibious operation, where vehicles may have limited opportunities for maintenance or resupply.That may explain why the newly seen vehicle appears to retain its autocannon alongside the laser and additional sensors.The combination would give crews more than one way to respond to a drone threat. A laser could be used when conditions allow, while the cannon could provide another option against targets that are difficult to engage with directed energy.The larger significance of the Type 19 variant may therefore lie less in the laser itself and more in how the PLA appears to be adapting armoured forces for a battlefield increasingly shaped by drones.If the vehicle eventually enters operational service, it could provide amphibious units with a mobile layer of counter-drone protection as they move towards and across Taiwan's coastline. But until more information emerges about its performance, power requirements, amphibious capability and operational status, its role in a future conflict remains uncertain.

articles.title: In 2001, a Houston baby needed a liver transplant as US flights were grounded; strangers moved the organ 800 miles by C-130, and 25 years later she is in law school
articles.summary: US News: On September 11, 2001, while the US was dealing with the attacks that killed nearly 3,000 people, a six-month-old baby in Houston was fighting for her.
articles.body: On September 11, 2001, while the US was dealing with the attacks that killed nearly 3,000 people, a six-month-old baby in Houston was fighting for her life. Kareena needed a liver transplant, but the donor organ was nearly 800 miles away in Nashville, and the civilian flights across the US had been grounded.The liver, packed in ice inside a box roughly two feet by one foot, eventually reached Houston aboard a C-130 cargo plane, Houston Chronicle reported. The aircraft, operated by the Tennessee Air National Guard, carried the organ from Nashville to Ellington Field. From there, soldiers took it to Texas Children’s Hospital, where doctors were waiting to perform the transplant.Kareena had been born with biliary atresia, a congenital defect in which the ducts that drain bile from the liver do not form. Because the bile could not drain properly, her liver became badly damaged at a very young age. By September 2001, she had spent most of her short life in the Texas Medical Center and was too sick to go home.“She was too ill to leave the hospital,” Dr John Goss, the hospital’s medical director for transplant services, told Houstone Chronicle, 25 years after the transplant. “She was very sick, and she wasn’t going to survive very long without a transplant,” he added.The chance of a transplant came on the night of September 10, when Goss received a call from his former colleague at Vanderbilt University, Dr Ravi Chari. A liver that could match the six-month-old’s size and blood type was available in Nashville.Transplant disrupted by 9/11The original plan was Chari would remove the liver in Nashville, Tennessee Donor Services would arrange a charter flight to Houston, and Goss would transplant the organ into Kareena.That plan changed the next morning. Goss was treating adult patients at St Luke’s when the first plane hit the World Trade Center in New York. He later recalled, “It’s weird. I can still remember we were in a patient room when the first jet flew into the tower.”A second plane hit the World Trade Center soon after. As the attacks unfolded in New York, Washington, DC, and Pennsylvania, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded every civilian aircraft in the country.In Nashville, Chari was still in the operating room with the donor liver. The charter flight that was supposed to carry the organ was no longer possible.Jill Grandas, who was then a coordinator with Tennessee Donor Services and is now its CEO, was told that the flight had been cancelled. A road journey to Houston was considered but rejected. At the time, the organ could not survive the roughly 12-hour drive.Grandas then went to the mail room, took out a phone book and called the air-traffic control tower at Nashville International Airport. She explained that a baby in Houston would die without the liver waiting in the operating room.The supervisor who answered understood the situation. Grandas later learnt that the woman had a relative on a transplant waiting list.Within minutes, another option emerged. The Tennessee Air National Guard agreed to fly the liver to Houston. “It was a feeling of joy in the midst of something so tragic,” Grandas said. “We were determined that we weren’t going to let another person die as a result of that attack.”Military plane carried the tiny liverNine National Guard members boarded a C-130 Hercules aircraft and flew the liver to Houston. The aircraft can carry up to 47,000 pounds, but on that flight its important cargo was a liver small enough to fit inside a box packed with ice.The plane landed at Ellington Field within a few hours. At noon, the organ was handed over to another group of soldiers. They drove it towards Texas Children’s Hospital in a military vehicle.The liver then reached Goss, who was waiting to perform the transplant. By that evening, Kareena had received the organ.“Even though there was the horrific event and it was meant to hurt a lot of people, there were still very good people who were not going to let it completely hurt us,” Goss said. “In the end, the good will win.”For Grandas, the successful journey of the organ was possible because everyone involved continued to find a way forward.“Nobody ever said no,” she said. “Not the staff at the hospital, not the FAA or the National Guard. We had a mission to get this liver to Houston. And we did.”Kareena remembers her savioursThe transplant gave Kareena the chance to grow up. Twenty-five years later, she is still living in the Houston area. She graduated from college and is now studying health policy in law school. She hopes to work in health equity. “I want to make the most of the life that so many strangers worked to give me,” she said.Kareena continues to remember the people who helped her survive. Every September 11, she calls Grandas in Nashville. The two met in person for the first time only recently, when Grandas travelled to Houston.On September 11, 2026, Kareena also returned to Texas Children’s Hospital, where Goss had performed the transplant 25 years earlier. The two have reunited several times since the surgery, although they had not met for a couple of years.Kareena greeted Goss with a hug and later took a selfie with him for her mother. But both said the story was bigger than their reunion.The liver had come from a Tennessee family that had lost an infant on the night of September 10, 2001. In the middle of that loss, the family chose to donate the infant’s organ so another child could live.“They didn’t just save a life,” Kareena said. “They created a family. They created friendships, communities,” she added.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: From one glass of milk to a 35-year legacy: How one Bihar tea seller’s kindness to babies became a family mission that lives on
articles.summary: At a small tea stall near the Rajgir Bus Stand in Bihar’s Nalanda district, a simple sign carries a message that has quietly touched thousands of live.
articles.body: At a small tea stall near the Rajgir Bus Stand in Bihar’s Nalanda district, a simple sign carries a message that has quietly touched thousands of lives: children from birth to 18 months can get milk for free. What began as one tea seller’s response to a mother struggling to feed her baby has continued for more than three decades. The story began in 1990, when Shravan Kumar was running his tea shop in Rajgir. According to reports by Hindustan and ETV Bharat, he noticed that some families visiting the area struggled to arrange milk for their young children. Instead of simply feeling sorry for them, Shravan decided to do something himself. He began providing milk to infants without asking their families for payment.A small tea stall with a big promiseShravan’s decision was simple: if a baby needed milk, the family could come to his shop and get it without worrying about the cost. According to Hindustan, the tea stall eventually became known for providing free milk to children up to 18 months old. The service was not presented as a temporary campaign or a publicity exercise. It became part of the shop’s identity. A board outside the stall informed people that milk was available free of cost for babies from birth to 18 months. ETV Bharat’s report gives a more personal account of how the initiative began. It says Shravan once heard a baby crying near his shop and realised the child was hungry. He gave the mother a glass of milk for the baby. When the child stopped crying after drinking it, the experience stayed with him. He then decided to continue providing milk to young children who needed it.What makes the story especially striking is that Shravan reportedly did not want others to finance the initiative. Oneindia, which also reported on the tea stall, says people offered donations after learning about his work, but Shravan chose to continue the service himself. For him, helping a hungry child was not something that needed recognition.After Shravan’s death, his brother kept the promise aliveShravan died in 2000, but the service did not end with him. His younger brother, Ranjit Kumar, popularly known as Tunna Baba, took responsibility for the tea stall and continued the tradition started by his brother. Hindustan reported in November 2023 that Ranjit had been providing free milk to children for 33 years, counting the years since Shravan first started the initiative in 1990. The story is therefore not simply about one generous tea seller. It is also about a family choosing to preserve an act of kindness long after the person who started it was gone. According to Nalanda Live, Ranjit said he distributes around 3 to 4 litres of milk every day, while the requirement can rise to around 10 to 15 litres during busy periods such as the Malmas Mela, when Rajgir sees a large number of visitors. The report also said that the family finances the service through its own earnings rather than relying on outside donations.“What will I take with me?”Perhaps the most powerful part of Ranjit’s story is his attitude towards money. Speaking to Nalanda Live, Ranjit reportedly said that he spends part of the tea shop’s earnings on the milk and does not feel the need to accumulate everything for himself. The report quoted him expressing the belief that material wealth cannot be taken along after death, while the blessings of people can bring a different kind of satisfaction. That philosophy has turned an ordinary tea shop into an unexpected place of support for families. The stall is located near the Rajgir Bus Stand, an area frequented by local residents, travellers and tourists. People who notice the sign can approach the shop when their young children need milk. Hindustan reported that visitors have also praised Ranjit’s work and shared pictures and posts about the initiative on social media.A legacy built one glass at a timeThere are many stories of charity that begin with large donations, organisations or fundraising campaigns. Shravan Kumar’s story began with something much smaller: a glass of milk. He saw a problem in front of him and chose to respond with whatever he could offer. His contribution may have appeared modest, but repeating that small act every day turned it into a decades-long tradition. Today, the Shravan Tea Stall carries the name of the man who started the initiative, while Ranjit continues to keep his brother’s promise alive. The story is a reminder that social service does not always require wealth, influence or a large organisation.Sometimes, it begins when an ordinary person notices someone else’s need and decides not to look away. More than 30 years after Shravan first offered milk to a hungry child, his family continues to serve young children at the same tea stall in Rajgir. And perhaps that is the most meaningful part of the story: his kindness did not end with him. It became a tradition.Looking for trusted parenting advice? There are many Union ministers from Bihar, but none has the influence to bring central help to Bihar," he said.Tejashwi also claimed that he had received no response to letters he wrote to PM Modi and Choudhary."Just like PM has ignored Bihar in times of flood, people will ignore him in the future," he said.The water levels of rivers in north Bihar have risen amid massive flooding in Nepal, from where several rivers flowing into Bihar originate.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 130 missing after Indonesian passenger ship sinks in Java Sea; 107 rescued, 6 dead - video
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Indonesian rescuers intensified a search in the Java Sea for 130 people reported missing after the passenger ship Virgo Transport 8 overturned and san.
articles.body: Indonesian rescuers intensified a search in the Java Sea for 130 people reported missing after the passenger ship Virgo Transport 8 overturned and sank in bad weather.At least 107 people were rescued and six bodies recovered after the vessel, carrying 243 people including 213 passengers and 30 crew members, lost contact with authorities early on Sunday.The ship had departed Surabaya in East Java on Saturday for Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan.I Putu Sudayana, who heads the Banjarmasin Search and Rescue Office, said the vessel’s captain had reported rough seas, with waves reaching up to three metres, before sending a distress message.“The ship’s operator reported the incident to authorities after receiving information that the vessel had encountered bad weather,” Sudayana said in a video briefing.The captain had reported that the vessel was listing before authorities received information that it had overturned and subsequently sunk, officials said.The Banjarmasin search and rescue agency said it received a report about two hours after contact with the ship was lost at around 2am on Sunday. The vessel’s last known position was about 148 kilometres from a pier in Banjarmasin.Search teams were deployed to the area, supported by four vessels, including a navy ship, as well as a helicopter. Nearby tugboats and other vessels also assisted in the rescue operation.By Sunday afternoon, rescuers had brought 107 people to safety and recovered six bodies, Sudayana said. The rescued passengers were transported on different vessels, with some expected to be taken to a port in East Java.Hundreds of relatives gathered at Banjarmasin’s Trisakti port command centre, checking passenger manifests and rescue lists as authorities continued efforts to locate those still missing.The Japanese-built Virgo Transport 8 was designed to carry both passengers and vehicles. Officials cautioned that the manifest figure may not reflect the actual number aboard, as passenger numbers on Indonesian ferries can differ from official records.Indonesia, an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands, relies heavily on ferries for inter-island travel. Maritime accidents remain a recurring concern, with safety enforcement frequently under scrutiny.The latest incident comes days after a ferry fire in the Philippines killed at least 76 people and left others missing. The latest accident follows another Indonesian ferry disaster last month, when at least 211 people were rescued from a vessel that caught fire in rough seas near Bali; one died and four remained missing. The incident happened less than two weeks after another Indonesian ferry, the Mutiara Sentosa 2, caught fire in waters off the main island of Java, leaving at least five people dead.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Road to key Yemeni city reopened after Houthis advance along Red Sea
articles.summary: A main access road to the city of Taiz in south-western Yemen has been reopened following an advance by Iran-backed Houthi rebels along the country's western...
articles.body:
Iran-backed Houthi rebels have captured the key port city of Mokha in Taiz province, giving them control of Yemen's entire Red Sea coastline.

Government forces still control parts of Taiz province, including the capital city of the same name, but fighting in the area continues with reports of attacks on Houthi positions.

The conflict in Yemen, involving Iran and Saudi Arabia, has left over 150,000 people dead from fighting and another 220,000 from indirect consequences, with 22 million people currently dependent on humanitarian assistance.

A main access road to the city of Taiz in south-western Yemen has been reopened following an advance by Iran-backed Houthi rebels along the country's western coast, local government and military sources reported on Sunday.

The Houthis now control the country's entire Red Sea coastline after capturing the key port city of Mokha in Taiz province from government forces earlier this week.

Mokha is located some 90 kilometres west of the city of Taiz. Government forces currently still control parts of Taiz province including its capital city of the same name, but fighting in the area continues.

Military sources said that government forces had again attacked Houthi positions in the Taiz area. Houthi-owned television channel Al-Masirah reported that Saudi Arabia had bombed targets to support pro-government forces.

According to Houthi-controlled news agency Saba, the Iran-backed rebels attacked weapons depots and command centres in Saudi Arabia.

The Houthis have been fighting Yemen's Saudi-backed government for more than a decade. A 2022 truce left the conflict largely frozen, but also with little prospect of an end to the war.

Fighting has flared up again amid the wider war involving Iran, plunging the already impoverished country, which borders Saudi Arabia and Oman, deeper into civil war.

According to UN estimates from 2021, more than 150,000 people were killed in fighting, while another 220,000 died as a result of indirect consequences of the war, including hunger and disease. Around 22 million people in Yemen currently depend on humanitarian assistance.

Their recent advance along the country's western coast will allow the Houthis to ramp up attacks and blockades on shipping launched amid resurging tensions with Saudi Arabia.

A Houthi spokesman said that shipping would remain safe, with the exception of Saudi vessels.

articles.title: Georgia killer who murdered two suburban real estate agents faces execution after 23-year wait for justice
articles.summary: Lori Brown's mother recalls the 2003 Powder Springs murders of two real estate agents as Stacey Ian Humphreys' Georgia execution date nears.
articles.body: As the execution date nears for a Georgia man convicted of killing two real estate agents, the mother of one victim is remembering the women who were murdered while simply doing their jobs, and the risks that real estate professionals still face. Barring a last-minute judicial stay or executive clemency, Stacey Ian Humphreys, 53, is scheduled for execution on Sept. 16 at the Georgia Diagnostic and Classification Prison in Jackson. On Nov. 3, 2003, Lori Brown, 21, and Cynthia "Cyndi" Williams, 33, were working from a model-home office inside the Oakwind subdivision, a rapidly growing, upscale residential development in Powder Springs, when Humphreys fatally shot them. The office welcomed prospective buyers, making interactions with unfamiliar visitors a routine part of their professions. 74-YEAR-OLD BECOMES FLORIDA'S OLDEST INMATE EXECUTED AFTER 1982 KILLING OF TEEN Williams returned to the office after lunch and encountered Humphreys first. Brown arrived shortly afterward and unknowingly walked into an armed robbery already underway. Humphreys held the women at gunpoint, made them strip, and killed them before fleeing with their ATM cards. There was no evidence of sexual assault. Ed Greathouse, a retired supervisory investigator with the Cobb County Judicial Circuit who assisted the prosecution, told Fox News Digital that investigators never determined why Humphreys chose that particular office over others in the development. A natural in real estate For Brown's mother, longtime real estate agent Linda Brown, her daughter’s outgoing personality made her a perfect fit for the profession. "Let me tell you, she was a rascal growing up," Linda told Fox News Digital. "She had a gregarious spirit about her." "She was a people person from the time she was small. She never met a stranger. That's why real estate was such a perfect place for her because she was really good at it." Brown formed a close friendship with Williams, who took Brown under her wing. She also planned to marry her high school sweetheart in 2004. She had been tasting wedding cakes and looking at venues, Linda said. On the day she was killed, her wedding-planning notebook sat neatly on her office desk. "Sometimes I think it's my fault. I should have never let her go in this direction with real estate but, you know, she was going to do what she was going to do," Linda added. Arrest and conviction After the murders, Humphreys used the stolen bank cards to withdraw over $3,000, according to court records. On Nov. 8, 2003, authorities arrested Humphreys in a rental Jeep Grand Cherokee, following a high-speed chase in Wisconsin. Investigators found the murder weapon inside the rental, along with Williams' blood on the gun. They found Brown's blood inside Humphreys’ personal vehicle, according to the Georgia Supreme Court record. Greathouse said investigators believed Humphreys was heading toward Canada when a Waukesha County officer apprehended him. "It was fairly common knowledge in prison, where he had been, and certainly in law enforcement, that if you get to Canada, Canada won't extradite you back to the United States, unless the prosecutor absolutely will not pursue the death penalty," he said. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X Although Humphreys insisted he did not remember killing the women, he told investigators, "I know I did it. I know it just as well as I know my own name." Authorities learned that Humphreys was behind on his vehicle payments and had taken out a high-interest payday loan he could not afford. In 2007, a Glynn County jury convicted Humphreys of two counts of malice murder, along with armed robbery, kidnapping and aggravated assault. He pleaded guilty to possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. THREE DEATH ROW INMATES EXECUTED BY LETHAL INJECTION IN RARE SAME-DAY STRING ACROSS US In favor of the death penalty The state scheduled Humphreys' execution for Dec. 17, 2025, but the State Board of Pardons and Paroles postponed the date and his clemency hearing amid legal challenges. Greathouse said obtaining a death sentence was unusual during his years working capital cases in Cobb County. SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS "I did 13 death penalty cases in Cobb County during my tenure, and that was, I think, one of two we actually achieved the death penalty," he said. "It's really rare." LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE Nearly 23 years after her daughter’s death, Linda remains skeptical that Humphreys' execution will take place. SEND US A TIP "Not only did we lose these two girls, but we had to go through 4.5 years waiting for a trial to come to an end. So, here we are 23 years later," she said. "I’m still in favor of the death penalty for this man that took their lives." Humphreys' attorney filed a motion this past week to try to throw out his death sentence over claims of jury misconduct, but a judge rejected that motion on Thursday, FOX 5 Atlanta reported. GOT A TIP? Safety for real estate professionals Linda continues to speak about the case during National REALTOR® Safety Month, an initiative held every September to raise awareness about safety risks in the profession. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST "A lot of my friends had said to me at that time, ‘We know you'll probably want to get out of real estate,’" Linda said. "I thought about it a long time, and I decided that I was not going to let this man drive me out of my profession." articles.summary: An Iranian cargo ship was struck early Sunday, Iranian state media reported, as the U.S.-Iran conflict marches on. Hossein Amir Teymoori, the governor of Qeshm, said an Iranian commercial container vessel was hit by an “unidentified projectile” near Hengam Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to the IRNA News Agency. The strike killed one…
articles.body:
An Iranian cargo ship was struck early Sunday, Iranian state media reported, as the U.S.-Iran conflict marches on.

Hossein Amir Teymoori, the governor of Qeshm, said an Iranian commercial container vessel was hit by an “unidentified projectile” near Hengam Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to the IRNA News Agency .

The strike killed one crew member and wounded four others, IRNA reported. Hengam Island is located roughly 1.2 miles south of Qeshm Island, the latter of which is the largest island in the Persian Gulf.

The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations organization also reported a vessel being struck in the strait, adding that a fire broke out on board and local authorities are helping evacuate crew members.

The U.S. has not taken responsibility for the strike. The Hill has reached out to U.S. Central Command (Centcom) for comment.

The Middle Eastern conflict , in its seventh month, continues without any sign of a deal to end hostilities. Earlier this week, Iranian and American forces exchanged fire, with the former launching missiles at Navy warships.

The U.S. military responded by destroying five Iranian oil tankers linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, per Centcom. The command said the Iranian regime “had used the tankers as part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC” and its proxies.

Iranian forces then launched a raid on an air base in Jordan overnight Tuesday into Wednesday. The Royal Jordanian Air Force operates the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, where U.S. personnel are stationed.

CBS News reported Thursday that the Iranian strikes damaged multiple American military aircraft, but President Trump denied that, telling NewsNation’s Robert Sherman the attack yielded “no damage” on assets.

Trump also predicted this week the war will end shortly after the November midterms, saying on Wednesday the Iranian regime “can’t hold out any longer.”

The president told reporters, “A negotiation could possibly happen, but it’s not something we’re looking at.”

articles.title: Trump tells Ukraine to stop targeting Russia’s diesel fuel
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has told urged his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelensky, to stop targeting Russia’s diesel fuel in its aerial attacks, claiming that it is “hurting the world.”
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has urged his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelensky, to stop targeting Russia’s diesel fuel in aerial attacks, claiming that it is “hurting the world.” A series of long-distance Ukrainian drone strikes has targeted Russia’s fuel infrastructure, hitting major processing plants and significantly reducing its refining capacity. “Mr Zelensky has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia. Let him go after targets, but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage of diesel,” Trump said during an official visit to Ireland on Sunday. “This isn’t done by the Middle East. This is done by what’s happening with Russia and Ukraine,” he claimed. His comments come as the ongoing war with Iran, which predominantly involves the United States, Iran and Israel, has caused global energy prices to surge. The crisis has particularly affected traffic through the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint. Global oil prices rose to $108 this week as fighting in the Middle East raises concerns about prolonged supply disruptions. US diesel prices have hit record highs, topping $6 a barrel Friday for the first time ever. Russia is the world’s second-largest exporter of diesel, behind the US, according to marine intelligence firm Kpler. Attack near Polish border Meanwhile both Russia and Ukraine are continuing to escalate their air war, with a Russian drone attack overnight into Sunday hitting a gas station in the northwest Ukrainian town of Yahodyn near the country’s border with Poland, Ukrainian authorities said. Attacks on gas stations have become so common that one Ukrainian network has started installing mesh cages around its facilities in the capital, Kyiv, to reduce the impact zone during strikes. The latest attack drew swift condemnation from Ukraine. “Russia’s barbaric strikes at the Ukraine-Poland border crossing point in Yahodyn are not just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders. This is Putin’s terror ‘knocking’ directly on the doors of the EU and NATO,” Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha wrote on X. The former prime minister of Sweden, Carl Bildt, said he had been on a train near the Polish border when a train behind his was targeted by a Russian drone. Bildt had been attending an international security conference in Kyiv known as the Yalta European Strategy (YES). “This wasn’t our train, but the one just minutes after us by the Polish border crossing,” Bildt wrote on X alongside a video appearing to show a drone hitting a nearby train as throngs of passengers evacuate. The border crossing was briefly shut but was operating normally again by 10 a.m. local time Sunday. Yahodyn is one of several Ukrainian-Polish border crossings through which a significant amount of military and humanitarian aid is delivered to the country. Zelensky in the past week alone, Russia had fired more than 2,000 drones at Ukraine, many of them jet-powered models, which are faster and more difficult to intercept than regular drones. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s military said it had struck an oil refinery in Russia’s Tatarstan republic overnight into Sunday. Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces said that it struck the TANECO refinery in the city of Nizhnekamsk, in an attack carried out alongside the Security Service of Ukraine and the Main Intelligence Directorate. Tatarstan officials said two civilians were killed and others injured in a Ukrainian attack on Nizhnekamsk. NATO countries, particularly Ukraine’s neighbors, are on high alert for military drones straying into their airspace. On Sunday, Lithuania said that a perceived drone sighting in its airspace prompted authorities to close Vilnius airport and NATO to scramble at least one fighter jet. The air alert was later lifted after the NATO jet identified the sighting as birds, Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Center said. A similar alert in Poland last week also turned out to have been triggered by birds.

articles.title: ‘Corruption, casteism, dynastic politics has ended’: Amit Shah hails 12 years of Modi govt

articles.body: Union home minister Amit Shah on Sunday said the Narendra Modi government had moved India away from corruption, casteism and dynastic politics and ushered in an era of “politics of performance”.Addressing a press conference to announce the ‘Seva Sankalp Abhiyan’, Shah said the month-long campaign would run from September 17 to October 17 to mark Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s birthday and “25 years of Modi rule in Gujarat and Centre”.Taking a direct jab at the Congress, Shah claimed that Indian politics had moved away from what he described as the three major scourges of the pre-2014 era — corruption, casteism and dynastic politics — towards a “politics of performance”.“Before 2014, Indian politics was suffering from three scourges -- corruption, casteism and dynastic politics. In the political era from 2014 to 2026, these three have ended and the people have moved the country towards a politics of performance,” Shah said.He added that the Modi government had also moved the country beyond what he described as “policy paralysis, coalition compulsions and poor decision-making”.The Union Home Minister also highlighted the government’s foreign and defence policies, saying India’s interests had been placed at the centre of decision-making.“For the first time in 12 years, the people have witnessed a foreign policy with a strong backbone. Whether it is our defence policy or our foreign policy, the guiding principle is ‘India First.’ India’s interests are paramount to us,” he said.Shah also cited India’s economic performance, saying the country had moved from the “Fragile Five” to the top five economies. “Recent first-quarter data shows India leading the major economies with a GDP growth rate of 7.8%,” he said.He further referred to the government’s policies on Indian languages, counter-terrorism and internal security.“We have demonstrated this to the entire world while addressing three long-standing issues—Article 370, Naxalism, and the situation in the Northeast—that had threatened the nation’s internal security for nearly five decades,” Shah said.The ‘Seva Sankalp Abhiyan’, whose slogan is “Jan Seva Hi Prabhu Seva” (public service is service to God), will seek to promote public participation in the goal of making India a developed country by 2047, Shah said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: How Gujarat's villagers turned mangroves into a natural coastal shield
articles.summary: India News: In the 1980s, when much of Gujarat’s coastline was losing its mangrove cover, some coastal communities began protecting the few patches that remained..
articles.body: In the 1980s, when much of Gujarat’s coastline was losing its mangrove cover, some coastal communities began protecting the few patches that remained. What looked like a small act of conservation would eventually become part of one of India’s most striking mangrove recoveries.Government data shows just how dramatic that transformation has been.According to the Forest Survey of India (FSI), Gujarat had around 427 sq km of mangrove cover in 1987. By 1999, that figure had more than doubled to 1,031 sq km. It reached 1,164.06 sq km in 2023, making Gujarat home to nearly one-quarter of India's mangrove cover. In 2026, the cover has grown to 1177.27 sq km.It attributes the growth to a combination of large-scale plantation programmes, public-private partnerships, community participation and better protection of existing forests.Mangroves are much more than trees growing in salty mud.Their dense network of roots holds sediment together, reduces coastal erosion and slows waves and storm surges before they can reach settlements further inland. The forests also provide breeding and nursery grounds for fish, crabs and other marine species, making them important to both coastal ecosystems and livelihoods.The numbers also reveal how significant Gujarat's recovery has become. The state's 1,164 sq km of mangroves in 2023 accounted for 23.66% of India's entire mangrove cover, second only to West Bengal.But the recovery has not been a simple story of trees being planted by the government. In several parts of Gujarat, conservation efforts have involved coastal communities in protecting and regenerating mangrove areas. That local involvement matters because mangroves occupy a difficult landscape — one constantly shaped by tides, salinity, grazing, cutting and human activity.The government has now taken the approach nationwide through MISHTI, launched in 2023 to restore and promote mangrove ecosystems along India's coast. Under the programme, mangroves are increasingly being treated as natural infrastructure — ecosystems that can perform some of the protective functions that would otherwise require expensive coastal engineering.Gujarat's story therefore offers an unusual lesson in climate protection: sometimes the most effective coastal defence is not something built against the sea.It is something that grows between the land and the sea.And in Gujarat, decades after villagers began protecting those seemingly insignificant patches of mangrove, they have grown into forests spanning more than 1,100 sq km — forming a vast, living barrier along one of India's most exposed coastlines.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Why Saudi Arabia has few options in its conflict with the Houthis
articles.summary: The Iran-backed Houthis’ swift advance in Yemen and attacks on Saudi Arabia have left the Gulf Arab kingdom with few options to respond, all of which carry heavy costs.
articles.body: The Iran-backed Houthis’ swift advance in Yemen and attacks on Saudi Arabia have left the Gulf Arab kingdom with few options to respond, all of which carry heavy costs. The key message emanating from the kingdom is that Riyadh does not want an all-out war, experts say, but the Houthis’ emboldened behavior may nonetheless drag the Gulf state into a wider conflict. All signs now “point to a large-scale Saudi retaliation, and that likelihood is increasing by the day,” Mohammed Al-Basha, an expert on Yemen and Washington, DC-based risk adviser, told CNN. “At this point they don’t have an option,” he said. This week, the Yemeni rebel group captured the strategic Perim Island, at the mouth of the Red Sea, along with the port town of Mocha as it sought to take control of the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a key energy route. Not long after, Saudi Arabia’s key oil pipeline was shuttered after it was attacked by drones from Iraq. No party has claimed responsibility but US President Donald Trump pointed the finger at Tehran, with Iranian proxies known to operate in Iraq. Saudi Arabia has been making greater use of the East-West pipeline since the Iran war effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, rerouting some 5 million barrels of oil per day that would have been destined for awaiting oil tankers in the Persian Gulf. It appears to amplify concerns expressed by the Kingdom early last month, a senior official telling CNN Saudi Arabia is bracing for a “multiple coordinated attacks” by Iraqi militias working with Iran-backed Houthis. On paper it appears a mismatch – wealthy Saudi Arabia on the one hand, with its well-equipped, modern military; on the other, a rebel group in impoverished Yemen. But the Houthis have proven exceptionally difficult to dislodge. Often seen by the West and some Gulf states as an Iranian proxy headed by a “rag tag” militia, the Houthis have spent years advancing their military and combat tactics. The group gained popularity among parts of the Middle East after striking Israel following the Gaza war, which was a result of the Hamas-led October 7 attack on Israel. The Houthis’ demands remain the same: They want an end to Saudi attempts to isolate the large swathes of northern Yemen controlled by the group through a travel and economic blockade. While they are allied with Iran, they also have their own agenda. Nasr al-Din Amer, head of the Houthi-run state news agency Saba, told CNN on Friday that the Houthis would continue “pressuring” Saudi Arabia until they “break the siege unjustly imposed by the Saudi enemy for 12 years” – pointing to a clear intention to climb the escalation ladder. Yemen was dragged into turmoil in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and drove the internationally recognized government into exile. Saudi Arabia led a military campaign the following year to dislodge the rebels and has continued to support the internationally recognized government while maintaining a crippling blockade against Houthi-held areas of the country. Iran, meanwhile, has supplied the Houthis with weapons and training and exercises some influence on the rebel group’s decisions. Despite its territorial losses, Saudi Arabia has not yet responded with full force, raising questions about its next moves. The kingdom’s actions in the coming days could mean a return to all-out war – as well as having major consequences for the US-Iran conflict. ‘Go all in’ The Gulf state is facing an Iran-backed group that is bent on expanding territorial control in Yemen. When it comes to options, it’s slim pickings for the Saudis. “Saudi Arabia really has limited options in the conflict with the Houthis,” Cinzia Bianco, a visiting fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, told CNN. One is to escalate, she said, but that carries hefty costs for the kingdom. If Riyadh does “try to go all in,” Bianco said, it could develop into an open-ended conflict similar to Yemen’s deadly civil war. That long-running conflict has turned Yemen into the world’s worst humanitarian crisis, with some 22 million people, roughly half of the population, now in need of humanitarian assistance. An all-out war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis would also be likely to drag in Iran, which has been at war with US since February. “It would be hard then to limit the conflict as purely a Yemeni situation rather than one chapter of the broader US-Iran war, in which Saudi Arabia would now enter as a combatant on the side of the US,” Bianco said. Meanwhile, the US is unlikely to step in militarily against the Houthis, especially amid the ongoing crisis in Hormuz, the upcoming midterm elections, and the domestic debate about the use of US resources in the Middle East. Trump is “in no position to double down on the commitment in the region at this political time,” Bianco said. Behind the scenes, the US has been resisting Saudi pressure to get involved in the renewed fighting. On Saturday, he said that the Houthis had called his administration and indicated they did not want the US to become directly involved in the conflict. “They would much prefer not having us involved, and they’re letting most ships go through. There’s just one country that they’re not too happy with, and we’ll get that straightened out,” Trump said. A source told CNN that the Saudi crown prince had spoken twice with Trump on Thursday and urged him to strike the Houthis as they advanced towards the Red Sea, but Trump declined. The US has, however, sent around 100 military advisers to Saudi Arabia to provide intelligence in its military campaign against the Houthis, CNN reported this week, citing multiple sources familiar with the effort. Nawaf Obaid, a senior fellow at the Department of War Studies at King’s College London and a former Saudi Arabian government adviser, told CNN that the “Saudi request was never for American airstrikes,” but only for intelligence. “To date, that support has been limited,” he said. ‘Exhausted the political solutions’ Another route is to try to find a political exit from the conflict, but it may now be too late for that option. Over the past few months, Saudi Arabia has exercised “strategic patience,” Bianco said, with Riyadh issuing repeated warnings and condemnations to both the Houthis and the Iranians, but to no avail. In response to the attack on its East-West pipeline, the Saudi foreign ministry said “the kingdom has chosen not to respond at this stage and to support the efforts of the Iraqi government,” from whose territory the attack was launched, but that it “reserves its right to take all necessary measures to safeguard its sovereignty.” Bianco said that Saudi Arabia has “exhausted the political solutions.” Even if Riyadh were to strike a deal with the Houthis, it would come at a great cost. Al-Basha said that would likely amount to complete submission to Houthi demands. “And that’s a very expensive submission. It’s basically surrender,” he said. It is unclear when Saudi Arabia will launch its next retaliatory move, but the repercussions are expected to surpass Yemen or Riyadh’s borders. “Backed by the Saudi-led coalition, the Yemeni government’s military campaign against the Houthis is already underway, and I expect it to intensify substantially in the coming days, or even hours,” Salman Al-Ansari, a Saudi geopolitical analyst, told CNN, adding that “we may also see major surprises on multiple fronts.” However, the Saudis will not launch an all-out war “without firm, sustained, and unequivocal international support,” Al-Ansari said. The international community had “made a serious mistake by failing to heed Saudi and Yemeni government past warnings” about the Houthis, he added. “Riyadh now expects the international community to correct course and fully support the liberation of Yemen from this malign militia.” Others say that, if the Houthis continue to escalate, the Gulf state will have to go to war – with or without international support. “The Saudis are under attack, from the Houthis, from the Iraqi Islamic Resistance – you don’t have an option,” Al-Basha said. “I’d hate to be in their shoes.” CNN’s Nic Robertson, Kylie Atwood, Katie Bo Lillis, Thomas Bordeaux and Zachary Cohen contributed to this report.

articles.title: US embassy child abuse images suspect flown from UK before police interview
articles.summary: The individual worked at the US embassy in Vauxhall, south London, had diplomatic protection, despite not being a diplomat.
articles.body:
A US embassy staffer accused of possessing indecent images of children, was detained at his south London flat and flown out of the UK in August, without being first questioned by British police.

The US Embassy confirmed to the BBC that authorities are investigating the allegations and they have reassigned the staff member to the US while inquiries continue.

"The United States government expects all personnel to adhere to the highest standards of conduct, and we take these allegations seriously," embassy officials said in a statement.

They added that they "quickly informed UK law enforcement and took swift action."

It is understood the individual worked at the US embassy in Vauxhall, south west London, and though not a diplomat, he enjoyed the umbrella of diplomatic protection.

He was flown back to the United States on a commercial flight, but their investigations are ongoing in conjunction with UK authorities.

It is also understood Home Office ministers and the Metropolitan Police are in close contact with the US embassy on this matter as investigations continue.

A UK government spokesperson said: "We expect all foreign diplomats in the UK to abide by our laws, in the same way we expect all UK diplomats to do so when posted overseas."

articles.title: Turkish police detain dozens in raids on gay bars and homes of LGBTQ+ activists
articles.summary: Human rights groups in Turkey have accused the government of using a family- values campaign to target the LGBTQ+ community.
articles.body:
Police in Turkey have detained 47 people in a series of raids on gay bars and the homes of LGBTQ+ activists, officials say.

Raids took place in 12 provinces over the weekend as part of a campaign dubbed "My Family is Safe" that the Turkish government says has been designed to protect family values.

One of the targets of the operation was LGBTQ+ association Kaos GL.

Same-sex marriage is not recognised in Turkey, with growing pressure on gay couples. Human rights groups in Turkey have accused the government of using the campaign to target the LGBTQ+ community.

Officers detained 26 people and seized drugs, digital equipment, smuggled alcohol and a firearm during the raids, according to the Istanbul chief prosecutor's office.

In a separate statement, the Ankara chief prosecutor's office said another 21 people had been detained as part of an investigation into Kaos GL.

The organisation said 50 activists had been detained, more than 10 taken after police raids on their homes.

It said that authorities had blocked several websites and social media accounts linked to LGBTQ+ organisations.

According to the group, authorities have accused Kaos GL of making "obscenity" in online posts that are available to children and had demanded the shutting down of the Kaos GL X account, as well as those of around 15 other LGBTQ+ organisations.

Same-sex relations are not an offence in Turkey but homophobia is common, with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan describing LGBTQ people as "perverts" responsible for the falling birth rate.

As part of "My Family is Safe", Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek says legal proceedings have been started against more than 160 people and a number of organisations and companies across the country.

Gurlek did not say how many people had been taken into custody, but said the raids came in the context of the "Decade of the Family" campaign.

However, the Turkish Human Rights Association says the Turkish government has been using the campaign to target the LGBTQ+ community in recent years.

"The real name of this operation is not 'My Family is Safe'; it is state-led discrimination, politics of fear and the dismantling of civil society," the organisation said on X.

articles.title: People fleeing Iran-backed rebels’ advance in Yemen describe a ‘hysterical panic’
articles.summary: It was a heart-pounding escape.
articles.body: It was a heart-pounding escape. As Houthi rebels backed by Iran swept south along Yemen’s Red Sea coast this week, some residents had little time to flee. “We set out in hysterical panic on a motorcycle, not knowing where we were heading,” Alaa Ali Salem said. “The roads suddenly became extremely congested, and while I was driving, the motorcycle overturned. My wife, my children and I were all injured.” His family and thousands of others, in numbers leaping by the day, are now displaced as the Arab world’s poorest country faces a potential return to a devastating civil war. The Associated Press on Saturday visited some of the newly displaced in Aden, a city under the control of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, as residents opened homes to them. Children sprawled in crowded rooms of thin mattresses that were scattered with the few belongings grabbed in haste. A young girl clutched a smartphone. Crutches were propped against a wall. Worn-looking elders napped. A fan stirred the air on a day where temperatures reached into the 90s Fahrenheit. Those fleeing have seen the front line of what the United Nations warns could be a return to a humanitarian catastrophe. The Houthis’ advance to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea threatens a key global shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has attacked some vessels during more than six months of war. But on the ground in Yemen, the rebels’ offensive means something very different. It could bring the kind of upheaval that killed 150,000 people and caused near-famine before a 2022 ceasefire. “This renewed war should alarm us all,” the U.N. special envoy for Yemen, Hans Grundberg, warned as the Houthis moved south. In Aden, a woman was in tears Saturday over what the ensuing chaos meant for her fragile family. “We saw soldiers shouting for a retreat as bullets flew all around, and we had no idea what was happening. One of my sons had a motorcycle, so I told him to take his children and flee,” said Durrah Ali Hassan, who took shelter in a relative’s house. She said she was worried about the toll on her pregnant daughter, who already had been bleeding. “I was so worried that roads might get blocked and that my daughter would die.” She was now in a coma at a hospital, her mother said. In just days’ time, the International Organization for Migration has revised its number of displaced people by 30,000 more, saying at least 76,000 people now have fled since July as fighting escalated. Iraq’s government confirmed that attacks that shut down a key Saudi oil pipeline on Thursday had originated from its territory. An umbrella group of Iran-backed militias in Iraq denied their involvement while praising the Houthis for their “ongoing battlefield victories against Saudi forces.” Regional officials have told The Associated Press that the Houthis and the Iraqi militias recently coordinated attacks on Saudi oil facilities. As the latest events threaten even higher global oil prices, U.S. President Donald Trump said Iran was “probably” responsible for the pipeline attack, but tried to calm concerns. “The Houthis called us, and they don’t want to fight with us,” Trump said. “They would much prefer not having us involved, and they’re letting most ships go through.” He said his administration has had “discussions” with the Houthis, but the White House didn’t say when. His administration engaged in at least one round of talks in May 2025. “We are not in war with Saudi Arabia, and the Houthis have their own problems,” Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told India Today TV on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in India. The Houthis are putting further pressure on neighboring Saudi Arabia, which backs the Yemen government fighting the rebels. While the Houthis have said they are only targeting Saudi shipping, oil markets remain wary. ‎Late on Saturday, the Saudi civil defense said a projectile fell in Al-Tawwal governorate near the border with Yemen along the Red Sea, injuring two people and damaging a mosque and several other buildings. The statement blamed the Houthis. There was no immediate claim of responsibility. As global shipping becomes even more challenged, Iran said a regional meeting is planned Monday between the foreign ministers of Gulf countries about talks between Tehran and Oman — located on the other side of the Strait of Hormuz — on managing shipping there. Commercial ship traffic remains low on what had been considered an international waterway before the war. Iran has expressed interest in having ships pay fees for transit. It has said traffic into the Persian Gulf would pass through Iranian waters, while the outbound route would pass partly through Iranian waters and partly through Oman’s. But Iran has said reaching an agreement with Oman on the strait doesn’t mean it will open for shipping. “The waterway would be opened up on the condition that the U.S. will terminate its blockade,” Iran’s president told the Indian broadcaster. The U.S. military on Saturday said its forces had redirected 100 commercial vessels over the past 60 days. Bahrain, however, said it will not attend any group meeting including Iran before the restoration of diplomatic relations between the countries.

articles.title: The fallout from the US-Canada trade clash transcends economic impact
articles.summary: Even more concerning is the prospect that the North America alliance could weaken while NATO also faces increasing strains.
articles.body:
The collapse of bilateral trade negotiations between the U.S. and Canada in late August has set off an escalation in tariffs that will be difficult to resolve. After the U.S. imposed a 50 percent tariff on a long list of Canadian goods through the never used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 , Canada followed with a 50 percent tariff on U.S. goods last week that will match the U.S. tariffs dollar for dollar .

Most observers are perplexed by what happened, considering the two parties were close to reaching an agreement. Some are still hopeful the dispute can be resolved, but no resolution is in sight, and President Trump has announced a ban on certain goods from Canada.

Several issues must be considered. First, what led to the breakdown? Second, what will the economic fallout be? Third, what are the broader ramifications of what is happening?

The backdrop is that negotiations to extend the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement got off to a rocky start when the Trump administration declined to extend the trade pact for a new 16-year term on July 1. This did not end the agreement, but it set in motion a wind down over a 10-year period if the parties cannot agree on how to amend it.

Not long after, the Trump administration announced 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods that were to become effective on Aug. 19. This purportedly was in response to retaliatory tariffs the Canadian government leveled on U.S. autos, alcohol and dairy products last year.

These developments left observers perplexed about what Trump is seeking. Many viewed the action as a ploy to gain leverage in negotiating changes in the trade agreement, which Trump once heralded as the most important trade agreement ever achieved. However, when the U.S. trade deficit did not shrink, Trump doubled down in his second term by implementing reciprocal tariffs against all U.S. trading partners, including Canada and Mexico.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer claims that Trump’s top priority for changing the agreement is to attain lower U.S. trade deficits with Canada and Mexico. However, this seems doubtful, considering its bilateral trade gap represents only 4 percent of the overall U.S. merchandise trade deficit .

A more plausible explanation is that Trump wants Canada to raise trade barriers to deter Chinese and other Asian countries from locating production facilities in the hemisphere, as Mexico did last year. Prime Minister Mark Carney, however, views this as an infringement on Canada’s sovereignty, and he felt he had no choice but to retaliate.

Beyond this, Trump is using tariffs to bludgeon America’s allies on issues that are unrelated to trade. Canada has shouldered a disproportionate burden, because Carney is willing to stand up to him . The Wall Street Journal editorial board has labeled Trump’s fight with Canada “ The Dumbest Trade War in History .”

The macroeconomic impact of higher U.S. tariffs is not likely to be major, considering that goods subject to the new duties totaled around 5 percent of all U.S. imports from Canada last year. Brad Setser of the Council of Foreign Relations estimates that the U.S. tariffs would generate about $10 billion in added tariff revenue. But he notes that the proposed deal would have lowered some of the earlier tariffs.

The impact of higher U.S. tariffs will be greater on Canada’s economy, because over 70 percent of Canada’s exports are to the U.S. For this reason, Trump believes the U.S. “ holds the cards ” and that Canada will capitulate at some point.

The New York Times reports that most Canadians want Ottawa to hold firm , however, even it prolongs economic pain. One tactic Canada is deploying in increasing tariffs is to target goods produced in border states such as Michigan, Ohio, Iowa and Maine that have significant exports to Canada.

The big unknown is how the trade rupture will play out. Some observers are hopeful that the two parties are near the stage where they are escalating before deescalating. This was the case between the U.S. and China following the “ Liberation Day ” announcement.

A Vox commentary, however, suggests that whatever Trump’s Canada fixation is, he seems willing to jeopardize his party’s Senate majority to get it. This suggests a stalemate could continue until after the U.S. midterm elections. If so, the toll the trade war takes on both countries could increase over time.

Even more concerning is the prospect that the North America alliance could weaken while NATO also faces increasing strains. The European Union reportedly is studying the tactics Canada is deploying in the event trade tensions with the U.S. heighten. Meanwhile, Bloomberg reports that the EU and Canada are forging a new, all-encompassing relationship ranging from trade to security, as they seek to build a new alliance to offset the influence of the two superpowers, the U.S. and China.

Nicholas Sargen, Ph.D., is an economic consultant and is affiliated with the Darden School of Business. The second edition of “ Global Shocks” is available now.

articles.title: Heavy rain floods New Jersey roads, leaves 5,600 without power; vehicles stuck in rising waters
articles.summary: US News: Heavy rain triggered flash flood warnings across parts of New Jersey on Sunday, leaving thousands of homes and businesses without power and causing fl.
articles.body: Heavy rain triggered flash flood warnings across parts of New Jersey on Sunday, leaving thousands of homes and businesses without power and causing flooding on roads in several areas.According to NJ.com, more than 5,600 customers were without electricity as of 7:50 am, based on outage reports from the state's four major utility companies. More than 2,000 outages were reported among PSE&G customers in Camden County.Vehicles stuck as floodwaters riseOfficials in Paterson reported flooded roads and vehicles stranded in deep water around 7:40 am. Some passengers were rescued from their vehicles, while a video posted on Facebook showed emergency services rescuing at least two people from a vehicle trapped in deep water.In Paramus, police said a vehicle became stuck in high water on Kalisa Way. The driver managed to get out of the vehicle before officers arrived.Flood warnings remain in effectA flash flood warning was in effect until 9:30 am for parts of Bergen, Essex, Hudson and Passaic counties, while a separate warning for Morris County remained in effect until 10 am. Most of the state was under a flood watch through noon, with storms expected to clear during the afternoon.Rainfall totals were expected to average 1-2 inches, with some areas potentially receiving 2.5-3 inches. Rainfall rates of up to 2 inches per hour were possible.The National Weather Service also issued a Flood Warning for the Saddle River near Lodi in Bergen County, effective through 4 pm Sunday. The river had reached 5.2 feet by 9:45 am, above its 5-foot bankfull stage, and was expected to rise to around 5.7 feet before falling later in the afternoon.The National Weather Service warned motorists against driving through flooded roads or going around barricades as heavy rain and rising waterways created dangerous conditions across parts of northern New Jersey.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: As Chavez and Maduro images disappear, is Venezuela entering a new chapter?
articles.summary: As part of Delcy Rodriguez’s ‘Venezuela reborn’ campaign, murals of leaders like Hugo Chavez are being removed.
articles.body:
Caracas, Venezuela – In a small square in central Caracas, Victor Rodriguez pauses at a giant mural of a figure draped in teal green. It’s the man he credits with giving him the opportunity to become an artist: former President Hugo Chavez.

Rodriguez, who paints under the name Forastero, helped create the image for the late Venezuelan leader's birthday on July 28. He says Chavez opened up new spaces for art and culture, giving artists from poorer neighbourhoods opportunities they never had before.

But today, Forastero is dismayed. He worries about the future of such art.

“Chavez represents revolution. He is anti-imperialist,” Forastero told Al Jazeera. “But now Chavez murals are disappearing.”

In recent months, Caracas has seen a transformation. Monumental images of Chavez and other figures linked to his political movement, chavismo, used to be common.

But now, graffiti, murals and billboards are being painted over or taken down. The Palace of Justice, once flanked by twin portraits of Chavez and the 19th-century revolutionary Simon Bolivar, has seen both images covered up.

In their place, there are new blue banners, emblazoned with the slogan "Venezuela renace" or "Venezuela reborn".

The changes come as Venezuela undergoes a period of political change after nearly three decades of chavista rule.

Since the United States launched a military operation to abduct and imprison then-President Nicolas Maduro in January, the country has been under intense pressure to reimagine its socialist government.

For some Venezuelans, the cosmetic changes are happening faster than any substantial ones. Some don’t want any changes at all.

Forastero sees maintaining his murals as a way of pushing back against the US influence in his government. “Now, painting Chavez is resistance," he said.

articles.title: US congressman swims to safety after his plane is forced to land on a lake
articles.summary: The small plane carrying Rep Tom Tiffany had a mechanical issue that forced the pilot to make an emergency landing on a Wisconsin lake.
articles.body:
Wisconsin Congressman Tom Tiffany has said he sustained minor injuries after a plane he was on landed on a lake, forcing him and the pilot to swim to safety.

Tiffany, the state's Republican nominee for governor, was travelling in a small plane on Saturday night when the aircraft encountered a mechanical issue, forcing the pilot to make an emergency landing in Lake Wausau, the county sheriff's office said.

Tiffany said he and the pilot called 911 once they landed.

"As the plane began to submerge, we exited the aircraft and swam to a shallow area, where we waited until emergency responders reached us by boat," Tiffany wrote on social media. The pilot also sustained minor injuries.

Tiffany was coming home from a dinner in La Crosse County when the plane suddenly lost power as it approached Wausau Downtown Airport, he said on Sunday.

Authorities received a 911 report of a plane crash on the lake at 20:49 local time (02:49 BST), the Marathon County Sheriff's office said in a press release. The pair managed to get out of the plane and to shallow water where a Wausau Fire Department airboat rescued them about 15 minutes later, at 21:05 local time, according to the sheriff's office.

The office said Tiffany and the pilot were the only two people on board the Beechcraft K35 - a single-engine plane, also known as a Bonanza, that can carry up to five people.

"God was watching over us tonight, and I am incredibly grateful to be here in the hospital with my wife, Chris, by my side," Tiffany said. "An experience like this reminds you just how precious life is."

He received a small cut over his right eye in the incident, his campaign said.

The cause of the mechanical issue was not immediately clear, and the sheriff's office said the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board will investigate the incident.

The plane remains in the lake as emergency crews work to remove it, the office added.

articles.title: Mecca Pact, but no troops yet: Pakistan expresses 'solidarity' with Saudi Arabia after Houthi attacks on kingdom
articles.summary: Pakistan News: The Mecca pact may promise “one for all, all for one”, but Pakistan is not putting boots on the ground just yet.Islamabad on Sunday expressed “complet.
articles.body: The Mecca pact may promise “one for all, all for one”, but Pakistan is not putting boots on the ground just yet.Islamabad on Sunday expressed “complete solidarity” with Saudi Arabia after a fresh wave of Houthi attacks on the kingdom, while warning that the strikes could threaten regional security and further disrupt global energy supplies.Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif conveyed Pakistan’s support to Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman during a phone call, according to the Pakistan Prime Minister’s Office.The outreach came a day after Saudi Arabia temporarily shut its 1,200-km East-West oil pipeline following a drone attack launched from Iraq.The pipeline is an important alternative route for Saudi oil exports as it allows crude to reach the Red Sea without passing through the Strait of Hormuz, where shipping has been severely disrupted by the wider US-Iran conflict since February.“While expressing complete solidarity with the Saudi leadership as well as the brotherly people of Saudi Arabia, the Prime Minister stated that the recent Houthi actions threatened regional peace and security and could further disrupt the global economy and energy supplies,” the Pakistan PMO said.Sharif vows to support peace effortsSharif condemned what he described as Houthi attacks on Saudi civilian and economic infrastructure, saying such strikes could further affect the global economy and energy supplies.He also said he, Pakistan’s army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar would continue efforts to reduce tensions and restore peace in West Asia.The Saudi crown prince appreciated Islamabad’s efforts towards peace and stability in the region, according to the PMO statement. The two leaders agreed to remain in close contact and expressed hope of meeting soon.The latest Houthi attacks have added to concerns over the security of Saudi energy infrastructure and alternative oil export routes amid wider disruption to regional shipping.Defence pact comes into focusThe developments have also revived attention on a mutual-defence pact signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye on August 7.Under the agreement, an armed attack against any one of the three countries would effectively be regarded as an attack against all three, with the pact also providing for enhanced defence cooperation.Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif had said on Wednesday that there should be no ambiguity over the commitment under the arrangement. He said an unprovoked attack on a member, or the spillover of the conflict in Yemen into Saudi Arabia, could activate the pact’s collective-defence provisions.However, Pakistan’s foreign ministry later clarified that no military response under the agreement was currently being discussed.Foreign ministry spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said, “There is no such thing under discussion right now ... When time comes (we) will act under the agreement.”Pakistan also said there were no immediate plans to expand the Mecca defence alliance.Houthi attacks and Red Sea escalationThe Houthi attacks have intensified as the Iran-backed Yemeni group has advanced along the Red Sea coast.According to news agency AP, the Houthis claimed further missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, while Saudi civil defence said a projectile fell in al-Tawwal governorate near the Yemen border, injuring two people and damaging a mosque and several other buildings.A Houthi military spokesperson, Brig Gen Yahya Saree, claimed that the group had targeted a military base in Saudi Arabia’s Najran region, although he provided no evidence or details on when the attack occurred.The escalation has also affected Yemen. The internationally recognised Yemeni government has vowed to regroup and fight back after the Houthis captured the port city of Mokha and other areas along the west coast.The International Organisation for Migration said more than 85,000 people had been displaced by the fighting since the beginning of the month, while more than 2,000 Yemenis had reached Djibouti after crossing the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.The Houthi advance has heightened concerns over the security of the Bab el-Mandeb, a crucial shipping route linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, at a time when the wider regional conflict has already disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
